Problem 510. The best route from Riverbend to Stone
A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.
Riverbend–Kite–Stone has segment costs [9, 10] (total 19); Riverbend–Iris–Birch–Stone has segment costs [8, 6, 5] (total 19); Riverbend–Oak–Stone has segment costs [12, 7] (total 19).
A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.
Which route should a traveler use from Riverbend to Stone, and why?
1. List the candidate routes and their segment costs. 2. All listed routes are open. 3. Add the segment costs for every feasible route. 4. The smallest feasible total is 19, on Riverbend–Kite–Stone.

River systems form directed networks: water has a direction, tributaries join larger streams, and upstream/downstream are relational concepts.

Clearwater flows into North Fork; Blue Creek flows into North Fork; North Fork flows into Silver River. A canal diverts some water from Blue Creek to a reservoir, but the remaining flow still reaches North Fork.
If river X flows into river Y, X is upstream of Y. Upstream relations can be followed through several confluences. Downstream is the reverse direction of flow.
Is Clearwater upstream of Silver River? Can water from Clearwater reach Silver River through the stated network?

1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: Clearwater→North Fork, Blue Creek→North Fork, North Fork→Silver River. 2. Follow arrows starting from Clearwater. 3. An arrow path reaches Silver River, so Clearwater is upstream of Silver River.
Yes; water from Clearwater can reach Silver River.
A river network can be reasoned about like any directed network; following the arrows is more reliable than guessing from names.
Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.
